lf-suggestion.description: One proposed change to content the user has already seen, with accept and reject controls.
lf-suggestion.instructions: Copy the current markup verbatim into lf-old and put the proposed markup in lf-new. Both slots replace, lf-new alone inserts, and lf-old alone deletes; a change to a widget also uses its complete old and new markup. Suggestions cannot nest, contain a draft, or appear in a reply. Set `resolves` to the comment whose thread should close when the user accepts. To withdraw an undecided suggestion, replace the whole `lf-suggestion` with `lf-old`'s contents. Keeping `lf-new`'s contents instead would accept it without the user's decision. When you work a decided suggestion into the surrounding prose, keep its surviving branch and its ids.
lf-suggestion.example:
Refill rules for the season:

Refill every feeder each morning.

Refill a feeder when its camera shows it half-empty.

lf-old.description: The current markup a suggestion proposes to replace or delete.
lf-old.instructions: Copy the current markup verbatim, including its ids. Omit this slot for an insertion.

lf-new.description: The proposed markup in a suggestion.
lf-new.instructions: Omit this slot for a deletion.

lf-age.description: How long ago a moment was, as “12m ago”, kept current while the page is open: for a time the reader weighs by its age, such as when a check last ran.
lf-age.instructions: Set `datetime` to the moment, with its seconds and its zone. On the page Leaf shows the age, and pointing at it reads the clock time in the reader's zone. Inside the element, write the time in your own words, which a reader sees wherever no script runs, such as a static export or the file opened without Leaf. Where you leave it empty, a static export shows the clock time there, with its zone, and the file alone shows nothing. An age changes width as it grows, and whatever follows it on its line, or takes its width from it as a table's column does, moves then: end the line with the age, or reserve its room in the page's CSS, with `display: inline-block` and a `min-width` (`page-layout.md`, "Space for changing text").

$languages.description: The code languages this layer can color, and how a filename maps to one. `names` is the full list, and build/vendor.mjs builds a grammar for each. A block of code names its language with a `language-…` class, as HTML recommends, by one of these names or an alias the grammar's build gives it, such as `py` for python; `page check` advises on a class naming any other, which shows uncolored, except `math`, whose LaTeX the runtime typesets as a formula. `paths` maps a file extension to a language, for widgets with no class to name one: a diff spans several files, and a file editor shows one. A file whose extension is not listed shows uncolored.
$languages.why-diff-is-not-a-path: `diff` is in `names` but not in `paths`. Coloring a .patch file inside a diff with the diff grammar would mark additions and deletions a second time, on top of the widget's own tints.

$data.description: Values from outside the markup that widgets display, replaced with `leaf data set`, which validates the whole value first. A named contract declares a value's meaning and JSON Schema; a widget declares its inputs with `inputs`, and markup binds an input to a source by the source's id. Values stay out of versions and the event log. A widget reads each through the property its input (`inputs`) names, and marks the records it draws with data attributes.

$keys.description: The meaning of each key an element declaration may carry, keyed by its name. Beside its `description`, a declaration holds the JSON Schema of its attributes under `attributes`, and each of its other facts beside them. A fact is declared rather than left to the widget's module because some part of Leaf needs it without running the module. The registry lint admits exactly these keys: it refuses a member for a key it does not admit, and a missing member for one it does. A layer may override a member to describe its own reading of a key, but cannot add a key. The site's registry reference is generated from this entry, in its order, so authors, the lint and the site read the same text.
$keys.attributes: The JSON Schema of the element's attributes, as Draft 2020-12 has it, which `page check` and message markup hold each occurrence to. It names each attribute in `properties`, and its other keywords, such as `required` and `dependentRequired`, constrain the attributes named there. Composing the vocabulary writes into `properties` the `id` every element takes, and each attribute an input binds by where the declaration doesn't name it there (`inputs`). It also writes `"type": "object"` and `"additionalProperties": false` into this schema and into a verb's `detail` schema ($verbs), so a declaration writes neither keyword in either, and each schema admits only what its `properties` names. An attribute schema may write `"additionalProperties": true` to admit attributes it doesn't name; a `detail` schema that writes any other value for either keyword is refused. A declaration with nothing to say about its element's attributes leaves `attributes` out, and the element then takes only the attributes composing the vocabulary writes for it, such as an optional `id`.
$keys.content: The element's content: `markup` (the author's markup), which is the default, `members` (only this element's declared member elements), `data` (one <pre> holding text in the notation the description names, with & < > escaped as & < >; an element leaves it out where its markup binds its `value` input, and may leave it out where it has a `value` input and its markup binds only other inputs), `markdown` (one <pre> escaped as for `data`, holding Markdown that Leaf renders as safe block Markdown read as a file, a soft line break reading as a space; a body record keeps the source, and passages read the rendered words), or `empty`. The server, `page check`, the passage reader and the first paint each read it.
$keys.verbs: Declares each verb of a widget that has state: the unit of state it changes, who writes it, and either its record (how the state reads in markup, $verbs.record) or the schema of its detail. A verb is the user's, sent from the page as `action` events, unless it declares `writer: "agent"`; the agent writes it with `leaf page report`, as `report` events. A user verb may create a child element (`creates`). An agent verb with `text: true` requires each report to carry a non-empty `detail.text`, a short note the report feed shows as written. The page marks a reported widget `data-lf-reported` until a version answers the report ($report). For each [widget, unit, verb] key, the latest action not taken back wins, and different verbs on one unit coexist. Leaf combines those actions with the authored values and hands the widget its complete state, keyed by verb, as `this.state`, which its `render()` reads. A past action keeps its key after the widget leaves the page. When an action of a widget that asks says its obligation is answered (`awaits`), and either records the answer itself (its verb is `awaits.value`) or turns the obligation from open to answered, Leaf records `meaning.answer` on it: the thread named by the widget's `resolves` attribute in the document the action came from, which the answer closes, or null. A decision whose outcome is the one its verb `withdraws` also records null, and the page reads as if nothing had been proposed. A verb with `decides: true` selects which members leave the page (`retired-when`); its required `outcome` field names the choice. An `outcome` field on any other verb is ordinary domain data.
$keys.awaits: The widget asks the user for input while its authored attributes match `when`, which puts an obligation on their list, On Me. The obligation's id is `widget:<source-id>` and never changes. `value` names the verb (`verbs`) whose state is the typed answer. Whether the obligation is answered is the widget's own word, its `answered` fact, which the declaration lists under `facts` with the schema `{"type": "boolean"}`. Its class may work the word out in a static `answered(state, element)`, as where a partial value can stand while the obligation is open, or an empty value can be a complete answer. Without one, the obligation is answered while the user's acts in force hold a state at that verb: one that records a non-empty value, or any action of a verb with no record. Either way only the user's acts count, never a value the markup holds. Leaf sends the word on each act and undo of the widget, refuses one that leaves it out, and draws the obligation answered or open in the gesture's own task. A widget whose word the page keeps none of asks, as one does before its first gesture and after a version restates any of its decisions. A tab's word can reopen the question, as when a version adds a step to a checklist, but only the user's gesture answers it. An answer written only into the markup answers nothing, so a version that settles a question there retires it (`retired`). `all` names the outcome one control can give every obligation of this kind at once. Once created, an obligation stays answered or withdrawn after `when` stops matching; an element that never matched creates none, and neither does a widget inside an exhibit (`exhibit`). A `restated` event asks again. While the agent owes a reply in a thread about the obligation, anchored inside the widget, or inside the group the author declares round it but no other obligation, the agent is its next actor and the obligation stays unanswered. A widget in a thread message keeps its obligation after the thread closes. A question the user answers in words is an agent message's obligation, not a widget's (`--obligation`). Any widget may declare it, whether bundled, from a package or a page's own; the user answers through its own gestures, and Leaf adds no answer of its own, such as a generic Done, to a widget or anything else On Me.
$keys.facts: What the widget works out of its state and markup for the page to keep, which `leaf page state` shows on the widget's element: each name is a static function of the widget's class, `name(state, element)`, called with the `state` Leaf sets and the widget's authored element, as `answerWords` is, and maps to the JSON Schema of the value it returns. Leaf calls each after each of the widget's actions and each undo of one, and sends the values on that event. Where the widget's state or markup moves without a gesture of the tab's own, as when a version or another tab's act reaches it, a tab showing the newest version calls them again and sends a `facts` event holding the values that differ from the ones the page keeps; the page admits it only where it changes one. The page keeps each fact's latest value, and a version that restates any of the widget's decisions lapses the widget's values until it says them again, so a value stands stale while no tab shows the version that moved it. Admission refuses a fact the declaration doesn't list and a value its schema refuses. A function that throws is the widget's failure, and its fact goes unsaid. Leaf gives meaning only to `answered` (`awaits`); the agent reads the rest.
$keys.retired-when: On a member: the outcome of its owner's decision that removes it from the page, as `accept` removes a suggestion's `lf-old`. Requires `owners`. The outcome is a value of the `outcome` field on the owner's one deciding verb. Leaf renders the decision itself, including its undo: it writes `data-lf-state="<outcome>"` on the owner and `data-lf-retired` on the removed members, which one theme rule hides. A widget reads the decision from its state, not these attributes. Once the log decides, `page check` lets a revision drop the member's ids, and `page check --render` reports a removed member that still shows words.
$keys.exhibit: `true` or `{when: {attribute: [values]}}`: the element shows content rather than asking, so widgets inside it never put an obligation on the user's On Me list, whichever form it takes. Where the element's attributes match `when`, by the presence and value rules of `awaits.when`, and always for `true`, the widgets inside are also quoted: they take no input, and delivery paints the element `data-lf-exhibit`. Elsewhere they take input but still ask nothing, as in an interactive sample. A module reads that mark before wiring input of its own.
$keys.history: `true`: the module renders the page's history, so a page that contains one is served the `history` reading with its state. The reading is the newest 50 logged events, newest first, each with who acted, what they did, the id of the thread it was in, whether a later undo took it back, and, for a widget gesture, the words its ids had when it was made. The module reads it with `readHistory`.
$keys.owners: The element declarations that may directly own this element. An owner's direct children of these kinds are its members, and a gesture on the owner's whole box stops at them.
$keys.refers: The attributes whose value names another element by its id, each mapped to an empty object, as an option's `for` is. An input's reference adds its attribute to them (`inputs`). In the browser a module passes the attribute to `navigateToDatum` to reach the named widget; it looks in the referrer's own document (its message, for a widget in a reply) before the page.
$keys.reading-role: The structural role the element plays, named by its required `label`. `pane` is a reading region whose body scrolls on its own while the workspace is full-height: it holds exactly one body element, optionally between a direct `header` and `footer`, and a visible heading goes in the header. `group` is a named group of what it holds, one part of the page that its label names wherever Leaf names it; a widget that asks inside it takes the innermost group as its question, the group's label as the question's words and the group as where going to the question starts. Validation and the obligation reader read this declaration, not tag names, so a package can contribute panes and groups under its own tags.
$keys.verbatim: `true`: the upgraded element keeps its authored words where they stand, so the passage reader reads them as the page's prose and a version comparison compares them; each nested widget's own declarations cover the words it generates. Without this key the passage reader treats the widget as opaque, since its module may insert, replace or reorder words: a comment's quote stays inside one of its authored children, and a data body it holds isn't read as words.
$keys.shadow: `true`: the module renders the page's words into an open shadow root, and Leaf's passage reading, selection capture and id lookups reach into it. A shadow root attached without this key, as a page script's own custom element attaches one, is opaque: its own words can't be quoted, and the passage reading reads its host by its light children.
$keys.inline: `true`: the element sits inline among the surrounding words. The render check therefore requires neither a width of its own nor a place where a block may stand.
$keys.visual: How a rendered picture offers Comment targets. Declaring it also tells the theme the widget is a picture (painted `data-lf-visual`), so an `lf-options` lays out options that hold one as it does options holding images. `whole` makes the picture one target. With `{prefixes: [PREFIX, …]}`, the module marks each part's node with `data-lf-part="ID"`, or states them as the element's `lfParts`, whose `read()` returns the current list of `{id, element, label, surface?}`; a comment on a part stores its id as `anchor.visual`. Leaf accepts as a part any longer id starting with one of the prefixes, such as `commit:3f2a` under `commit:`, and the rest of the picture stays one target. `surface` may name a descendant whose own paint, without decoration, gives the outline Leaf marks; `element` stays the target for hits and travel. A comment whose part is gone detaches on replay instead of widening to the whole picture. A visual that draws its parts over time also gives `reveal`: `reveal(id)` must synchronously show a state that holds that part, cancelling any pending change that would remove it, and Leaf calls it before going to the part from a thread or `navigateToDatum`. While a declared part is missing from the current state, its threads sit on the whole picture. A visual with too many parts to list, such as a chart's points, also gives `find` and `at`: `find(id)` returns the record for one part of the current state, drawing an element for it if it must, or null, and Leaf asks it rather than searching `read`, which may then list none, since `read` is what the target picker and a screen reader's list offer; a part it doesn't find sits on the whole picture, since the visual may draw it once it can, as a chart draws no point before it has room; `at(node)` returns the part a node of the visual stands for where no element `read` names holds it, or null: Leaf asks it for a hit, as on a line through the data, and for the visual itself when focus on it names a target, as the point a chart's keys reached. A visual whose parts are no places to stand also gives `focus` and takes focus for them itself: Leaf calls `focus(id)` as it places focus on the visual for part `id`, travelling there or handing the user back from a comment on it, and at no other time, and the visual settles on the part, as a chart moves its reading to the point. Dispatch a bubbling, composed `lf-layout` event on the element after any change to rendering or geometry, including an attribute or style change in place. The render check validates each record.
$keys.views: An object with members, a CSS selector matching direct authored children shown one at a time, and optional parts: true for a page's parts. Delivery carries the selector; the browser owns their membership and hidden attribute from first paint onward; authored hidden does not select a view. openingView returns the fragment's member, else the tab's saved member, else its supplied fallback (first member by default); reload prefers the saved member. keepView both shows a member and remembers it, or shows none when passed null without forgetting the last member. Its optional third argument keeps an outgoing member visible for an animation without selecting or saving it. A parts holder stands directly in a main with no Layout, each member holding its own Layout. module-state.md, "State only this tab keeps", owns view-state behavior, and what Leaf keeps of the open member: its name in the address and the user's place in it.
$keys.space: The width past the reading measure the element takes in a column or sidebar Layout: `wide` takes the shared, capped width for a block slightly wider than the column, from the prose's start edge; `available` takes all the width the page shell can give, into both margins. Without it the element fills its container, as every element does in other Layouts; an element read as lines of text keeps to the measure in its own stylesheet (`max-inline-size: var(--lf-measure)`). An authored element may override it with `data-width=wide|available`, which the theme applies without moving the prose.
$keys.height: The height in CSS pixels the page reserves for the element before its module draws: the declared number, or an authored `data-height`, which overrides it; `true` reserves only where `data-height` is given. The theme holds the box to it from first paint until the module marks the element drawn (`lf-rendered`). Declare it on a widget whose drawing can't be sized from its markup. A module that can draw at any height, such as a chart's, draws at this one, so nothing moves; for content with its own height, the reserved height is the author's estimate of it.
$keys.bound: The element has its own height and scrolls inside it, so a long log or feed never grows the page. `start` opens at the first line; `end` follows the newest entry while the user is at the end, and stays where the user scrolled back to otherwise. An authored element may set or override it with `data-bound=start|end`; delivery writes it as `data-lf-bound`.
$keys.spine: `true`: the element can rest as a spine, a box too narrow for words, and show the rest of itself over the page when the reader points at it, focuses inside it or arms go-to, as `lf-toc` rests as the contents spine. On a screen under a mouse, a sidebar before a `layout-column` body whose track holds only this element narrows to that spine rather than taking a column's room, so the prose starts beside it, and the Layout lets what the element shows lie over the body. Anywhere else the element fills its box as any other does.
$keys.flow: `true`: the element draws no box of its own around its authored blocks, so in a column or sidebar Layout they stand in the page's flow, as a `section`'s do: words keep the prose's start edge, a block declaring more room takes it, and the element's box grows round that block. `{when: {attribute: [values]}}` makes it so only while those authored attributes match, by the same rules as `awaits.when`, as a tab set written `flow="page"` draws no frame and a boxed one does. Where it holds, the element has no width of its own, so a `data-width` written on it has no effect; it belongs on the block that needs the room.
$keys.inputs: The widget's named typed data inputs. Each names a $data.contracts contract and at least one of the two attributes markup binds it by: source names the attribute holding a page source id, and reference the attribute holding a widget's id. Naming an attribute as source or reference declares it: composing the vocabulary writes it into the attribute schema's `properties` as a string, unless the declaration gives it a schema there, and writes a reference's attribute into `refers`. So a declaration names such an attribute once, here, and lists it in `attributes` only to require it or to say more of it than that it is a string. The input reads the one output of its contract that the named widget declares (`outputs`); `page check` refuses a widget with none or more than one. Markup binds the source or the relation, never both. Leaf leaves the property of an unbound input to the widget, except that a `content: data` element's input whose property is `value` reads the text of its `<pre>`. A document binds each source to one contract; later documents may rebind it and read the value against their own contract. Optional property names the element property Leaf sets to the delivered value, or null while there is none; a module reads the input only there, never through a package-owned source name, and dispatches drawn naming that property and the value it drew once its marked records stand. Optional measured names the widget's receipt attribute, which the declaration requires beside the source attribute (`package check` names a declaration that doesn't), tying the value written in the element's content to the source run that produced it: when the source holds a different run, `page check` warns that the measurement is stale, and `page state` reports it. Rewriting the source counts as a new run even with the same value; age alone never makes a measurement stale.
$keys.outputs: What the widget holds for other widgets to read: each output is a property of its element, under the output's name, typed by one $data.contracts contract. The module sets the property to the complete value, or null while it has none, and then dispatches `change` on the element, as a form control does for `value`. Another widget's input (`inputs`) reads it by naming the element (`reference`) and binds by contract. A tag that declares more than one output of a contract passes `package check`, and `page check` refuses each input of that contract that names an element of that tag. An output lives with its element in the browser: it reaches neither the server nor the agent, and has no source revision or run receipt.
$keys.example: Authored markup exhibiting the element, valid against the merged registry: an agent reads it with the element declaration and writes from it, and `page check`, `page init` and `package check` name one a page could not hold.
$keys.instructions: Instructions for an author using this element, read after choosing it and before writing markup. One non-empty string, separate from the short `description` and the attribute schema.

$attributes.description: The attributes that mean the same on every widget, as HTML's global attributes do. Leaf supplies each one's meaning, so no key maps a widget's own name for it. A declaration lists `label`, `tone` and `resolves` (`verbs`) among its `properties` when its element takes them, like any other attribute. Composing the vocabulary writes in the other three, so a declaration doesn't list them: `id` on every element, where a declaration says only whether `required` names it; `restated` ($restated) on a widget with a user verb that keeps one state for the whole widget ($verbs.unit); and `overruled` ($report) on a widget with an agent verb. An element that another widget's verb names by id, as a board's `move` names a card, lists `restated` itself.
$attributes.label: The element's name, which the page uses to name the element elsewhere, as On Me and the activity feed do. An option card, a board card, a group, a column and a tab take it; a section is already named by its heading and a disclosure by its summary. Whether the element shows its name is the element's own: a column and a tab draw theirs, and a card or a group shows whatever title its author writes in it. An attribute the element merely shows first, such as a metric's value, is not its name.
$attributes.tone: One of the layer's semantic tints. Composing the vocabulary gives the attribute `$tones.names`, which the theme has a rule for, as its `enum`.

$verbs.description: The meaning of each field a verb (`verbs`) may declare, one member per field. The registry lint holds these members to the fields it admits, as it holds `$keys` to a declaration's keys.
$verbs.attention: `true`, on a user verb: changing this verb's state, including repeating an action or undoing it, asks for the agent's attention even when no obligation changes. Use it for optional commands the agent should act on, such as Archive; it creates no obligation on the user's On Me list and no required reply. Without it, an action asks for attention only when it changes obligations or work the agent has in hand. Admission reads the active page's declaration and records the decision on the event, so later versions cannot remove an admitted request from delivery. A version's note settles a recordless action's receipt; a later change to its state still asks for attention.
$verbs.unsent: `true`, on a user verb: the verb records what the user is still working on and hasn't sent, such as a playground's settings before its submission. Its actions are no update: they ask for attention only by changing an obligation, and never count as work the agent has in hand on the widget. The agent reads them in page state, and a delivered message about the widget carries, as `unsent`, the action in force when the user wrote it (`delivery.DELIVERY`). A verb declares `attention` or `unsent`, not both.
$verbs.unit: On a verb that declares a `detail` schema and keeps a state for each member: the required string detail field that identifies the member, by element id or data key, as `add`'s `option` does. A verb that leaves `unit` out keeps one state for the whole widget, as `choose` on an `lf-options` does. A verb with a position record leaves it out too, and keeps a state for each member its `detail.unit` names. Composing the vocabulary writes `unit` into both, as `"widget"` and as `"unit"`, so a declaration writes it only to name a field of its own.
$verbs.detail: The JSON Schema of the action's `detail`, for a verb with no `record`, whose state is then the detail of its action in force, shaped as the widget defines it. A verb declares a record or a detail schema, never both, and one that `creates` a child declares a detail schema. Composing the vocabulary writes the schema's `type` and `additionalProperties`, as `$keys.attributes` says.
$verbs.writer: `"agent"`: the agent writes the verb with `leaf page report`, as `report` events ($report). Without it the user writes it from the page, as `action` events. An agent verb declares an `attribute` or `value` record, so a version's markup can be compared with the report, and creates no child.
$verbs.text: `true`, on an agent verb only: each report carries a non-empty `detail.text`, a short note the report feed shows as written.
$verbs.decides: `true` declares the widget’s one deciding user verb: it folds by widget and requires a string-enum `outcome` in its detail. That outcome selects which members retire (`retired-when`) or withdraws the proposal (`withdraws`). Other verbs may use an `outcome` field without deciding semantics. Obligation answers remain the conditions in `awaits`.
$verbs.withdraws: On the deciding verb: the outcome that declines the proposal. It answers the obligation without closing the widget's `resolves` thread. A revision may also remove an unanswered proposal outright, whether or not it has retirable members; ids from earlier versions don't prevent it.
$verbs.contract: An optional instance binding `{field, attribute}` on a custom-detail verb. The widget declares `attribute` a string, and composition gives it the data contract name grammar. Its authored value names one $data.contracts entry whose schema also validates the entire detail `field`; the package’s base detail schema still applies. An absent attribute keeps the base schema. Page checks refuse unknown contracts, and admission reads the binding from the immutable document that sent the action. This selects an instance’s payload contract without replacing the widget declaration.
$verbs.creates: A verb (`verbs`) that adds a child element declares `{child, words}`: `child` is the tag it creates, and `words` names the detail field holding the child's text; the verb's `unit` field holds the child's id. The user typed that text, so it reads as inline Markdown, as a message does, each line break a line. While the action is in force, the widget has that child; undoing or retracting the action removes it. Admission records the child's tag in `meaning.creates`, so a reader without the registry still knows what the action made, and refuses an id the sending document already uses. It also stores the verb's state definition in `meaning.state`, so a later incompatible definition doesn't change how the action reads.
$verbs.record: How the state reads in markup. `{attr}`: one scalar in the unit's own `attr`; `detail.value` takes that attribute's schema, so the log and the markup can't disagree. This is the `value` kind, and composing the vocabulary writes `kind: "value"` into a record that names no `kind`. A value record may add `property`, the element's property that holds the value on the page, and with it `event`, the event the element dispatches when the user changes the value, `change` unless named: Leaf sets the property from the state and records it on the event, so a component written without Leaf records from its declaration alone (`module-plain-elements.md`). `{kind: "attribute", attr}`: the elements inside the unit that carry `attr`, as the list of ids in `detail.value`, an array even where the widget allows one. `{kind: "body"}`: the unit's own words. `{kind: "position", within}`: where the unit sits in a `within` container. `detail.unit` names the moved member (never the widget), `detail.value` the container, and `detail.rank` its sort key there: a base-36 fraction, digits 0-9a-z not ending in 0, compared as a string, ties broken by id. Authored members rank by authored order, and a widget computes a dropped member's rank between its new neighbours with `rankAt` from `runtime/lib/rank.js`. The rank places the member in the same gap while later revisions author the container the same way. A revision that authors it differently absorbs the move: the member is written where the move left it, and the move can no longer be undone. Admission refuses a move made on an older revision whose container the newest one authors differently. Two tabs dropping into one gap get equal ranks, and the id order can put the later drop outside that gap. Leaf starts from the authored value (null for an absent value attribute or a verb with no record, the authored ids for an attribute set), applies the actions in force and the user's unsent updates, and renders the complete state without resetting or rebuilding the DOM on undo or refusal.

$report.answering: By explicit id. `page stamp` adds a report to the version note's `settles` list when the stamped revision writes in its reported state or marks its element `overruled`, and from that revision on the report no longer applies. A revision that changes nothing answers nothing, so the report stays shown.
$report.overruled: A boolean attribute on the reported element, which every widget with an agent-written verb (`verbs`) takes ($attributes): this revision keeps its own state over the report in force. It belongs only to the revision whose stamp overrules; the stamp records the answer on the version note, so later revisions leave it off.
$report.feed: All reports form one feed, in log order. Each entry carries its target, action, detail, optional text, speaker, time and version, and one disposition: `effective` (part of current state), `outranked` (a newer report on the same key takes precedence), or `settled` (named in a version note). Work the agent has in hand is not a report: it is an update's Working stage or a started to-do.
$report.wakes: A report joins the watcher's batch: `leaf wait` prints it with the user's updates, the same `ack` confirms it, and `leaf page close` is refused while one is unread. The user's On Me doesn't count reports, which are news the agent owes the page.

$settlement.description: The `settles` list on a version note ends provisional facts the agent supplied. Each entry is `{kind, id}`, so ids of different kinds can't collide and a new kind needs no new note field. The list is explicit and permanent: time alone ends nothing, and a later note need not repeat an entry.
$settlement.report: The id is a report event. Stamping adds one for each report whose state the source writes in or explicitly overrules.
$settlement.todo: The id is an open to-do on a page widget. `page stamp --completes <widget>` adds one for each to-do on that widget opened before the stamped revision, ending it as `done`, and lets the revision remove the widget.
$settlement.why-restated-is-separate: `restated` is not a settlement. It retracts a user decision because the authored words or state it rested on changed, while `settles` completes provisional information the agent supplied. Merging the two would make finishing work look like taking back the user's action.

$awaits.description: The meaning of each field `awaits` may declare, one member per field. The registry lint holds these members to the fields it admits, as it holds `$keys` to a declaration's keys.
$awaits.value: The user-written verb (`verbs`) whose state is the obligation's typed answer: a recorded verb's value, or a custom verb's full current detail, as a map by member id for a verb that keeps state per member.
$awaits.when: The authored attributes that make an element ask: a map from each attribute to the values that make it one, `true` for its presence and `false` for its absence, regardless of its value type. Every attribute named must match. `lf-options` declares `{"settled": [false]}`, so it asks until it is `settled`, and `lf-draft` declares `{"required": [true]}`, so a draft asks only where its author marks it. Without `when`, every element of the tag asks, as every `lf-suggestion` does.
$awaits.all: The outcome a blanket yes gives, where one control answers every obligation of this kind at once (`Accept all (3)`). It must be an `outcome` of the widget's deciding verb, and the module must expose a method named for that verb taking the outcome, so each obligation records its own decision. Without it, the user answers each obligation where it is.
$awaits.retired: The `when` attribute an author sets to end an obligation already asked, as `settled` ends an `lf-options`' obligation while its options stay on the page with their context. `when` must ask only while the flag is false. `page check` counts an element that fails `when` on this flag alone as asked, not as one that never asks.

$restated.description: A boolean attribute saying this revision rewrote words the user already decided on, so the decision no longer applies and the user is asked again. Put it on the element the decision rests on: an `lf-draft` or `lf-suggestion`, the `lf-card` or `lf-option` inside a board or an `lf-options`, or an `lf-options` whose question you rewrote, which then waits on an answer given after the stamp. It retracts every action that named that element: a rewritten card drops only that card's moves, while a rewritten option takes back the whole pick it was part of.
$restated.why: Decisions are recorded against the revision the user saw and survive ordinary edits, so change presentation and wording directly. Use this attribute only when the decision itself should no longer apply; the log records the retraction and keeps the original answer.
$restated.when: When a revision makes a decision no longer apply and needs a fresh answer, write the new content, mark the element the decision names, and say why in the stamp note. Changing decided wording or presentation alone needs no marker. An unused or repeated marker does no harm.
$restated.once: Put the marker only on the revision that retracts the decision; stamping records the retraction. Leave it off later revisions unless they withdraw another decision.
$restated.example: Adds --dry-run to every mutating command. It defaults on for `purge`.

$series.description: The categorical colours this layer paints a chart's series in. The theme defines them as `--lf-series-1` through `--lf-series-N`, and `steps` is N: how many series a chart can tell apart, and the count the palette check holds the tokens to. A project that adds a step raises `steps` here and adds the token in its theme. A chart with more series than steps merges the small ones or splits into several charts, since two series in one colour mislead. The list stops at five because further steps can't stay distinct for users with colour-vision deficiency.

$reactions.description: The emoji Leaf offers as reactions, in the order the reaction lists show them and their digit shortcuts press them. A reaction is a `comment` or `reply` carrying one emoji in place of `text`, a message like any other (`events.md`, "Reactions"): the agent may send any emoji, and the user picks from this list. The kernel offers none, and a package that changes the list restates it whole.

$tones.description: The semantic tints this layer paints, and the full list an author may use: validation refuses any other word, and the theme has a rule for each. A widget takes a tone in its `tone` attribute ($attributes), and composing the vocabulary writes this list into that attribute's `enum`, so a new tag taking a tone needs only to declare the attribute. The list is short on purpose: a page that can tint anything conveys nothing, and the palette supports three. The author decides which facts get a tint, since only the author knows whether a value is good news; `ok` on one page and `danger` on another may mark the same word.

.lf-scroll.description: A box the page's CSS scrolls, such as a wide trace given `overflow-x: auto`. Leaf contains its positioned descendants and adds keyboard access and continuation cues when its content exceeds it, measuring this box rather than every descendant. The page's CSS owns its overflow, including at breakpoints. Leaf fits an image, SVG or video to its container, so give media inside the box `max-width: none` to keep its drawn width.

svg.lf-drawing.description: A schematic the page draws itself as inline SVG, such as a layout or a mechanism, inside a `<figure>`, with `role="img"` and an `aria-label` stating its point for a reader who can't see it. Use no `<title>`: the browser shows it as a tooltip over the whole drawing. Paint its marks with these classes, whose colors follow the theme: `.frame` and `.frame-head` for a window or pane and its header; `.box`, with `.hot` for the one that matters; `.line` (`.soft`) for a line of text; `.highlight`; `.ghost` for where something would go; `.guide` and `.dim` for alignment and dimension lines; `.arrow`, with `.tip` (`.hot`) on its marker; `.mark` for an accent dot and `.glyph` for the character on it; and `.ok`, `.warn` and `.danger` fills. Text is muted; `.strong`, `.small` and `.mono` restyle it. Without a `width`, the drawing fills its figure; give a thumbnail one. For a mark particular to the subject, add a page-local class that uses the same tokens.

.lf-lede.description: The opening paragraph, set slightly larger.
.lf-lede.example: One paragraph saying what this page decides.

.lf-tag.description: An inline chip label. Add `ok`, `warn` or `danger` to draw it in that status tone.

.lf-callout.description: An aside set off from the prose by a tint, for something the user must not miss. Add `ok`, `warn` or `danger` when it reports a status, as `class="lf-callout warn"` for a paused release; the tint and the title take the tone, and the prose keeps the body's ink. The title is a `<strong>` written as the callout's first child; one opening a paragraph stays in the body's ink. In a flow wider than the column, such as a sidebar page's body, it keeps the prose width; one holding a wide chart or table takes `data-width`.
.lf-callout.example: <aside class="lf-callout" id="rollback-note">Rollback is one flag flip; the backfill is idempotent.</aside>

pre.lf-terminal.description: A terminal session: each command a `<b>` holding its prompt, its output plain beneath it, an `<i>` on a line of its own where output was cut, and a `<mark>` on the part of the output the reader should notice. The command reads in bold and the cut in the code's muted ink, and long lines wrap rather than scroll sideways. Put it in a `<figure>` with an `id` and a `<figcaption>` that says what the run shows.

section.lf-panel.description: A titled region on a sidebar page (`<main class="layout-sidebar">`) holding one thing, such as a table, a log or a list of steps, under a short heading that names it. The heading and spacing group the region without an enclosing card; its contents keep their own visual structure.

.lf-facts.description: A grid of labels and values for summary facts, written as a definition list.

.lf-metric.description: A metric tile: one figure under the label that names it, with an optional change beside the figure in a `<small>`, written as a one-term definition list. A row of them goes in a `layout-tiles` block. It is set as type under a hairline rather than as a card; restyle it through the theme's tokens.
.lf-metric.example:
open failures
2 change: -1
sample duration
4 min

td.lf-numeric.description: A table cell holding a quantity, right-aligned so the figures in a column line up on their last digit. Put `class="lf-numeric"` on the column's heading cell too, or the heading sits left of its figures. Add the class to each such cell yourself. Leaf doesn't infer it, since "60" and "60 sessions" look alike.

button.description: A press for an action your page's own script handles. On a page that wears the reading face, as a page in the `reading` theme does, it wears the face of Leaf's own buttons, so the page's controls and Leaf's read as one set: `type="submit"` frames the action that commits the page's work, as Leaf's Send and Done are framed, and a toggle sets `aria-pressed`, whose `true` draws it selected. A page without the face keeps the browser's button. Give a control of the page's own design its look in page CSS, which outranks the face.

input, select.description: A labeled field or choice for the page's own script. On a page that wears the reading face, as a page in the `reading` theme does, a text field and select wear the face of Leaf's own fields, matching its buttons, and a radio or checkbox written inside its `<label>` wears Leaf's choice: the label is the hit area and carries the focus ring, and the mark shows selection without a box around it. Group radios by name. A page without the face keeps the browser's controls. Arrange the row in page CSS, which also outranks the face where a control is of the page's own design.
input, select.example:
<label for="preview-case">Conversation</label>
<select id="preview-case"><option>Short exchange</option><option>Long exchange</option></select>
<label><input type="radio" name="detail" value="summary" checked>Summary</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="detail" value="full">Full detail</label>

table.description: Rows of one shape compared column by column, such as runs per configuration. On a page that wears the reading face, as a page in the `reading` theme does, columns size to their content, and a table wider than the measure wraps its cells, or scrolls inside itself once they can wrap no further, so set no widths or wrapping on it or its cells; a page without the face keeps the browser's table. Under the face, put identifiers such as test names and paths in `<code>`, which can break inside a cell; a bare identifier is one unbreakable word that holds its column wide and squeezes the others. `page check --render` warns when a table scrolls sideways while one of its cells wraps. A bare `<th>` is a column heading, drawn as a small muted label; `<th scope="row">` names a row, in bold at the body's size, and a `<code>` name that is all it holds stays whole, up to a third of the column. Add a `<caption>` when the section's heading doesn't say what the columns mean. For a few headline figures, put each figure in its own `dl` inside a `layout-tiles` block instead, and alternatives the user picks between in a widget that asks for the pick.

hgroup > p:first-child.description:
The `

` that opens a heading group, before its heading: an eyebrow, the short label above the heading, set in small capitals on a page that wears the reading face, as a page in the `reading` theme does; a page without the face keeps the browser's paragraph. A `

` after the heading, a subtitle, keeps the body's face.

details.description: Native disclosure with a clickable <summary>; find-in-page reaches the collapsed content. `page-authoring.md`, ‘Reading cost’, owns when to use one.

pre > code[class*=\"language-\"].description: A literal the user can select and quote, such as a command, a config file or a snippet of output. To color it, add `class="language-NAME"` with a name from `$languages`; leave the class off where the body is in no language, such as a log. A walkthrough with numbered lines, highlighted ranges or remarks at a line belongs in a code widget that draws them instead.
